title: CFA Ethics 43: Using third-party research - the responsibility stays yours
subtitle: Vetting the source, understanding the method, and when diligence counts as sufficient
whyItMatters: Nobody does every piece of analysis themselves, so this question applies to almost every recommendation you have ever made - yet most learners only think of Standard V(A) when building a model of their own.
openingQuestion: You use a report from a reputable research house as the basis for your recommendation. What does Standard V(A) require?
openingOptions: Nothing further, since that house already has a reputation
Vetting the methodology and whether it is sound
Only citing the source clearly in your own report
Redoing the entire analysis yourself from raw data
explanation: Standard V(A) permits relying on someone else's research, but not transferring responsibility to them. How much diligence is needed depends on the circumstances: a house with a proven process you have used many times requires less than a new source, or one with an obvious conflict of interest. The minimum questions must always be answerable: what assumptions does the research rest on, where does the data come from, is anyone paying for this research, and is the conclusion consistent with what you know about the business. If you cannot answer them, you are issuing a recommendation with no basis of your own.

summary.keyIdea: Citing the source and having a reasonable basis are two separate duties: the first handles who wrote it, the second handles why it can be believed.
summary.commonMistake: Citing thoroughly and treating that as the job done. Citation solves plagiarism, not reasonable basis.

application.title: What has to be done
application.message: Check the provider's process: where they get their data, who validates it, whether they have been wrong before. That is the part of the diligence that cannot be skipped.

sections.text: Using someone else's research is normal and necessary - nobody can analyse everything themselves. Standard V(A) permits it, but does not permit transferring responsibility to them.
How much diligence depends on the source

A house with a proven process you have used many times demands less diligence than a new source, or one with an obvious conflict of interest. This is a principle of proportionality rather than a fixed threshold.

sections.label: Four minimum questions
sections.text: What assumptions does the research rest on? Where does the data come from? Is anyone paying for this research? Is the conclusion consistent with what you already know about the business? If you cannot answer them, you are issuing a recommendation with no basis of your own.

items: Research paid for by the company under analysis: this brings in Standard I(B) on independence too, so the funding must be disclosed rather than merely the content vetted.

Two reputable sources reaching opposite conclusions: a signal to dig deeper, not evidence that one is wrong. Picking the one that matches the conclusion you already hold is confirmation bias dressed as research.

sections.text: The same report, used two ways

left.label: A violation
left.text: A broker sends a report recommending BUY on a steel stock. You pass that recommendation straight to clients, citing the source clearly. But you do not know the report assumes iron ore prices hold flat for three years, nor that the broker has just underwritten an issue for that same company. Full citation does not save it: the reasonable basis for the recommendation you issue is still your duty.

right.label: Not a violation
right.text: The same report, but you read the assumptions, see that the ore price is the decisive variable, check it yourself against futures data, discover the underwriting relationship and disclose it to clients. You may still reach exactly the broker's conclusion - the difference is that you now know what you are relying on.

sections.label: The level of diligence varies with the source, not with the conclusion
sections.text: A provider with a proven process you have used for years and cross-checked demands less. A new source, one paid for by the company under analysis, or one whose conclusion diverges sharply from what you know about the business - all three demand a deeper look. The easy mistake is lowering the diligence when the report agrees with the view you already hold.

lines: Citing the source solves the copyright question.
It does not solve the reasonable basis question - that one is still yours.

diagram.label: You may rely on third-party research
You may not transfer responsibility to them
Diligence varies with the source: familiar or new, conflicted or not
Unable to answer the minimum questions means no basis at all

realWorldExample.company: Three questions that quickly filter a research source
realWorldExample.description: Who paid for this research - if it is the company under analysis, Standard I(B) comes into play as well. Is the method described in enough detail for someone else to verify - a conclusion without a route to it cannot be vetted. And does the conclusion contradict any other source you trust - a contradiction does not itself prove error, but it is a signal to dig deeper before relying on it.

quiz.question: When you use third-party research, where does responsibility sit?
options: With the research provider, if they are a recognised reputable house
With the research provider, since they are the author of the original analysis
Split between the two in proportion to their contribution
Still with whoever issues the recommendation, and it cannot be transferred
quiz.explanation: Being allowed to rely on it does not mean being allowed to hand over responsibility - that is the core distinction in Standard V(A).

quiz.question: What does the necessary level of diligence depend on?
options: Whether the source is familiar or new, and whether it is conflicted
The length of the research report being used
The fee you paid for access to that research
Whether the research has been published publicly or circulated privately
quiz.explanation: The standard is reasonableness in the circumstances - a source used many times with a verifiable process demands less than a new one.

quiz.question: Which question belongs to the minimum set you must be able to answer?
options: What date in the year the research was published
What assumptions the research rests on and who paid for it
How many other institutions in the market also cite that same research
What professional qualifications the author holds
quiz.explanation: Assumptions and funding are the two things that bear most heavily on whether the conclusion can be trusted.

quiz.question: What about research paid for by the company under analysis?
options: Usable as normal, provided the source is cited clearly in your own report
Not usable in any form whatsoever
Standard I(B) on independence comes into play alongside V(A)
Only needs vetting if the conclusion is a Buy recommendation
quiz.explanation: Two standards apply at once, and that raises the diligence required rather than merely adding a citation line.

quiz.question: What does a conclusion contradicting another trusted source mean?
options: Something normal that needs no further handling
Evidence that one of the two sources has miscalculated
A reason to drop both sources from your analysis
A signal to dig deeper, not yet evidence of error
quiz.explanation: A contradiction between two credible sources usually points to a differing assumption somewhere - and finding it is the most valuable part.

keyTakeaways: You may rely on third-party research, but you may not transfer responsibility
Diligence varies with the source: familiar or new, conflicted or not
Minimum questions: what assumptions, what data, who paid, is it consistent
Research paid for by the company under analysis brings in Standard I(B) too
A contradiction between sources is a signal to dig, not evidence of error

practicePrompt.question: You used an industry forecast from a consultancy in your valuation. You then discover the forecast was commissioned by the very company you are analysing. What should you do?
options: Leave it, since the consultancy is an independent party
Re-examine the assumptions and disclose who funded it
Drop the entire valuation section built on that forecast
Leave it but add a small note about the funding
practicePrompt.explanation: Dropping it entirely overreacts - research commissioned by an issuer is not automatically wrong, and Standard I(B) accepts the model where it is disclosed. But a small note is not sufficient under VI(A). Three things have to happen together, and finding a source to cross-check against is what turns a recommendation resting on borrowed basis into one with a basis of your own.
